intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis with neurologic defects (SDCHCN) is caused by mutation in the SLC2A1 gene (138140) on chromosome 1p34.2.

paragraphs.text: Stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis (sdCHC) is a rare form of stomatocytosis. It is associated with a cold-induced cation leak in red cells, hemolytic anemia and hepatosplenomegaly, together with cataracts, seizures, mental retardation and movement disorder (Flatt et al., 2011). Red cell membranes are deficient in stomatin (Fricke et al., 2004). Flatt et al. (2011) and Bawazir et al. (2012) found that the disorder is caused by mutations in the SLC2A1 gene, which encodes GLUT1. In the patient reported by Bawazir et al. (2012), the extremely cation-leaky red cells caused hemolysis and pseudohyperkalemia.

paragraphs.text: Fricke et al. (2004) described 2 patients with stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis. In both patients, the passive red cell K+ leak was lowest at around 20 to 25 degrees C, so the cells were extremely leaky at 0 degrees C. Both patients had a congenital syndrome of mental retardation, seizures, cataracts and massive hepatosplenomegaly. Fricke et al. (2004) suggested that this probably defined a new haemato-neurological syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Bawazir et al. (2012) described an infant with GLUT1 deficiency and a cation-leaky red cell state. The infant presented with erratic hyperkalemia, neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, anemia, hepatic dysfunction and microcephaly. Seizures developed later, and developmental milestones were delayed. Brain MRI and CT showed multiple abnormalities, including periventricular calcification. Visual impairment resulted from cataracts and retinal dysfunction.

paragraphs.text: Lande et al. (1982) studied erythrocyte membrane proteins from 2 patients with congenital hemolytic anemia caused by increased erythrocyte membrane permeability to Na and K. One patient had hereditary stomatocytosis and the other had cryohydrocytosis. On one-dimensional SDS gel electrophoresis, the 28,000-dalton band 7 component was reduced in both patients. On two-dimensional electrophoresis, this component resolved into 2 proteins, 22 x 8 and 60 x 8. Protein 22 x 8 was completely absent in both patients, whereas 60 x 8 was present.

paragraphs.text: Fricke et al. (2004) described 3 new isolated cases and 1 new pedigree of hereditary stomatocytosis, and gave further details on 1 previously reported case. In every case, Western blotting of red cell membranes showed a deficiency of stomatin, the 32-kD membrane protein. All cases had pronounced cation leaks at 37 degrees C, with markedly abnormal intracellular Na+ and K+ concentrations. Immunocytochemistry showed that the stomatin deficiency was not complete: some red cells were stomatin positive, and all platelets and neutrophils were stomatin positive.

paragraphs.text: Fricke et al. (2004) found that stomatin-deficient cases of hereditary stomatocytosis differed markedly in how the passive K+ leak depended on temperature. Three cases showed a simple monotonic temperature dependence. The other 2 cases had a minimum at 20 to 25 degrees C, which is the cryohydrocytosis phenotype. Only these 2 cryohydrocytosis cases had the associated neurologic syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Bawazir et al. (2012) suggested that the multisystem pathology probably reflects 2 effects. The first is deficient glucose transport at the blood-brain barrier, as in typical GLUT1 deficiency. The second is the harmful osmotic effect of a cation-leaky membrane protein in cells that express GLUT1, notably red cells.
